# Latin {#sec-latin}

*Pater Noster.* For most of European history this was the Lord's Prayer — not
one version among several but the text itself, memorised by people who spoke no
Latin, and the vehicle through which the prayer reached every western European
language in this book.

## Roman Missal

The liturgical text, used in the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours.

::: {.prayer lang="la" speech="la" #la-missal audio="Read aloud=assets/audio/pater-noster-spoken.mp3; Gregorian chant=assets/audio/pater-noster-chant.mp3" audio-credit="Recordings from Wikimedia Commons: reading by Geremia (public domain); chant by <a href='https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Schola_Gregoriana-Pater_Noster.ogg'>Schola Gregoriana</a> (CC BY-SA 3.0)."}
| Pater noster, qui es in cælis:
| sanctificétur nomen tuum;
| advéniat regnum tuum;
| fiat volúntas tua, sicut in cælo, et in terra.
| Panem nostrum cotidiánum da nobis hódie;
| et dimítte nobis débita nostra,
| sicut et nos dimíttimus debitóribus nostris;
| et ne nos indúcas in tentatiónem;
| sed líbera nos a malo.
:::

The acute accents are not classical: they are the Missal's stress marks,
printed to tell a reader which syllable to lean on when chanting. Before the
1962 edition, *cotidianum* was spelled *quotidianum*.

Latin is the one chapter with real recordings rather than a synthetic voice —
no browser ships a Latin voice, and the language has been sung for long enough
that a recording is the better witness anyway. The **Listen** button offers a
plain reading and the Gregorian setting; both come from Wikimedia Commons.

## Vulgata Clementina

Jerome's text as fixed by the Sixto-Clementine edition of 1592.

::: {.prayer lang="la" speech="la" #la-vulgate .variant}
| pater noster qui es in cælis
| sanctificetur nomen tuum
| adveniat regnum tuum
| fiat voluntas tua sicut in cælo et in terra
| panem nostrum supersubstantialem da nobis hodie
| et dimitte nobis debita nostra sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris
| et ne nos inducas in tentationem sed libera nos a malo
:::

The one substantive difference is in the fifth line. The Missal has
*cotidianum*, "daily"; the Vulgate has **supersubstantialem**, Jerome's
literal attempt at the untranslatable Greek ἐπιούσιον — "super-substantial",
bread beyond substance. Jerome used it in Matthew and *quotidianum* in Luke,
for the same Greek word, and the liturgy followed Luke.

In the *Nova Vulgata*, the official Latin Bible of the Catholic Church, the
last word is capitalised — *a Malo* — indicating the Evil One rather than
abstract evil.

## Editorial variants

The four editions of the Vulgate differ here only in small ways. The Clementine
has *ne nos inducas* where the *Nova Vulgata* has *ne inducas nos*. The
Stuttgart Vulgate reads *qui in caelis es* for *qui es in caelis*, *veniat* for
*adveniat*, *dimisimus* for *dimittimus*, and *temptationem* for *tentationem*.

## No doxology

The Latin liturgy has never joined *for thine is the kingdom* to the end of the
prayer, and neither does the Vulgate — agreeing, as it happens, with the modern
critical editions of the Greek. It does appear in the Roman Rite Mass as
revised in 1969, in the form *quia tuum est regnum, et potestas, et gloria, in
saecula*, but separated from the prayer by the embolism, *Libera nos,
quaesumus…*
